📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1698 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

Sources indicate that JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

Sources indicate that LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

Sources indicate that the LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

It has been revealed that safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Recent findings suggest that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

Recent findings suggest that LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

Recent findings suggest that LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Industry observers note that tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

In a recent development, that's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

According to recent reports, this is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. I think these technical requirements are notable when estimating the cost to hire an LLM engineer, particularly for specialized enterprise projects. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. #8497. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2472 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model.
  • Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

In a recent development, similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

It has been revealed that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Sources indicate that text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

It has been revealed that in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

According to recent reports, pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

It has been revealed that available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Let’s get our model to call some tools.

Industry observers note that in this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

The easiest way to run Inkling 2 locally is with the Llama App, available for macOS and Windows. After you have installed it on your computer, select your preferred GGUF quant on the Hub, click the "Use this model" button and select "Llama".

It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so.

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

Sources indicate that SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

It has been revealed that MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

Here’s an example CLI invocation:.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

It has been revealed that build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

Industry observers note that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

Sources indicate that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

Sources indicate that the photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

Industry observers note that we have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

According to recent reports, we are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

Tech Report: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API with Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Sources indicate that frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock.
  • The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock. The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings, Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP).

Sources indicate that frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings.

The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place.

It has been revealed that EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both programs.

In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup.

It has been revealed that A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps.

Anyone with access to the trusted access program API can list the offerings and check their status for an account, an organization in AWS Organizations, or an Amazon Bedrock project. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility.

Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation.

Industry observers note that with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), you can retain your data in your own AWS environment with full control. It is designed with over 100 customers, including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility, like healthcare, financial services, and law.

Recent findings suggest that automated safety monitoring looks for patterns that only show up across many requests. These include intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm, such as offensive cyber operations. They also include agents that go beyond what a user asked for, such as using a software exploit to reach an internal system.

In a recent development, on Amazon Bedrock, AWS operates EFS and the customer inputs and outputs stay within the customer’s AWS account. Only automated safety monitoring within AWS reads the retained inputs and outputs. AWS human reviewers don’t review content for EFS. Your review stays with you. Neither AWS nor Anthropic humans access your retained inputs or outputs. Your inputs and outputs are never used for training.

Amazon Bedrock reaches your AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket as a single AWS service principal and only through the key policy and bucket policy that you write. You can remove that access at any time, but Amazon Bedrock stops serving the covered models 24 hours after it loses access to your key or bucket.

Figure 1: EFS workflow on Amazon Bedrock.

When you call a covered model including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP):.

Industry observers note that A Case summarizes what automated safety monitoring found and references the related transcripts. Retained records arrive under the transcripts/ prefix in your bucket, and case files arrive under review-cases/. Your team reviews each Case and writes a response file to review-responses/, stating whether it found a violation (violation or no_violation) and, for a violation, the applicable policy category.

Recent findings suggest that EDC offers the same automated safety monitoring as EFS and human review of flagged activity stays with your team. Unlike EFS, EDC stores retained data in Amazon managed storage, encrypted with AWS managed keys, so there’s no bucket or key to set up. Eligible customers can access both EFS and EDC through a single enrollment application. If your policy allows retained data to stay in Amazon-managed storage and encrypted with AWS-managed keys, enroll in EDC. If your policy instead requires retained data to be encrypted with your AWS KMS key and stay in your S3 bucket, enroll in EFS. Either way, your team will be able to review flagged activity.

Outside EFS and EDC, you can use Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock in two ways today:.

Recent findings suggest that with EFS, retained data is stored only in your own S3 bucket, encrypted with your KMS key. Neither Anthropic nor AWS keeps it in their own storage. The following table compares EFS with the other routes.

Table 1: Routes for Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock.

Storage configurations apply to one Region at a time, and a Region without a configuration uses Amazon-managed storage. Save a configuration in every Region where you call covered models.

Start by checking your EFS status with the trusted access program API:.

It has been revealed that if the status is eligible, your account is approved. If it’s requestable, follow the steps in the statusReason field to request access. Joining the preview turns off zero data retention for the accounts you add.

After you’re approved, set up EFS in each Region where you call covered models:.

It has been revealed that the EFS documentation has the complete key policy, bucket policy, IAM policy, and API calls for each step. It also covers organization and project configurations, and troubleshooting. To use enterprise data controls instead, skip steps 1 and 2 and choose Amazon-managed storage in step 3.

The trusted access program API, now generally available, gives you one way to find model provider offerings on Amazon Bedrock, check your status, and enroll, with IAM policies and SCPs controlling who can opt in. EFS and EDC are the first offerings in public preview. They give you control over your data when you use Claude Fable and Cyber Verification Program models. With your own Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon Bedrock keeps no copy of the retained data, your AWS KMS key encrypts it, and every access appears in your own AWS CloudTrail logs.

To get started, check your EFS status with aws bedrock list-trusted-access-programs and enroll in the EFS preview. To learn more, see the trusted access programs documentation and the EFS/EDC documentation.

To enroll in the EFS and EDC public preview, work with your AWS account team to submit a request. Have the AWS account IDs ready (or Amazon Bedrock runtime project ARNs for projects) and note that the preview is for customers already enrolled in EFS ZDR.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. Breaking: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

According to recent reports, in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

Sources indicate that AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 reveals a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

In a recent development, figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

According to recent reports, there are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

In a recent development, at the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, declared in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

It has been revealed that we work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

In a recent development, figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel reveals what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Recent findings suggest that claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no latest work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Recent findings suggest that adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote fresh instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

In a recent development, checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Sources indicate that shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model stated it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to newly introduced spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also reveals the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

Recent findings suggest that the shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

It has been revealed that public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

In a recent development, for example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

It has been revealed that harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

In a recent development, balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Sources indicate that table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

Recent findings suggest that in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

It has been revealed that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

According to recent reports, what a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a fresh harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

It has been revealed that that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask newly introduced questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 indicates the setup.

In a recent development, figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

According to recent reports, table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

In a recent development, before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

It has been revealed that we ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

Recent findings suggest that the model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

It has been revealed that we built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

According to recent reports, the D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

Sources indicate that the original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Sources indicate that figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the upcoming parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

It has been revealed that the shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Sources indicate that before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

In a recent development, it is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

Recent findings suggest that the adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

It has been revealed that several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Sources indicate that harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

Industry observers note that when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each latest model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 indicates the raman-lab results for each model.

Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

Recent findings suggest that the comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

In a recent development, figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Sources indicate that the comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

According to recent reports, task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Industry observers note that task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Recent findings suggest that environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

It has been revealed that agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no latest work.

Recent findings suggest that rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each newly introduced task.

It has been revealed that evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The latest work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Industry observers note that agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

Recent findings suggest that D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Recent findings suggest that evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

According to recent reports, no-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

In a recent development, rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Sources indicate that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.
