⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added four latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed.
  • A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path.
  • It has been revealed that NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

For simulation and training, prepare:.

A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.

Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.

For physical-robot testing, prepare:.

Recent findings suggest that A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.

A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.

A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.

It has been revealed that install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:.

Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:.

Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

Recent findings suggest that at each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

It has been revealed that goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

According to recent reports, figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Sources indicate that rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

Industry observers note that the obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py, ToF sensing is in sensors.py, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/.

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below demonstrates selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

In a recent development, the 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.

Run this command to train the policy:.

Sources indicate that figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation.

Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements.

Navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash// relative to the repository root. Choose a model_.pt file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.pt below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording.

In a recent development, playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model.

Industry observers note that figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays.

These deployment tools run the navigation model on a laptop and send adjusted gamepad commands to the walking policy on the robot. Use the same walking policy that was used during navigation training.

Section 1 saves the walker’s ONNX export to .pretrained_checkpoints/rsl_rl/https/omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Assets/Isaac/6.2/Isaac/IsaacLab/PretrainedCheckpoints/rsl_rl/exported/policy.onnx, relative to the Isaac Lab repository root.

Load that walking policy using Pollen’s policy-loading guide. The deployment README includes the transfer steps, including how to package an ONNX export that uses an external data file.

From your Isaac Lab checkout, set up SSH access and check inference with the robot standing upright and still:.

Dry-run copies the helpers and streams sensor data, but sends no movement commands. Watch the proposed commands as obstacles enter the sensor’s view. Keep the navigation ONNX and any companion .data file together.

Once those checks pass, start supervised gamepad navigation:.

Hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Forward speed is capped at 0.15 m/s by default, with an additional close-obstacle brake and stale-input stopping. Start in a clear area and verify stopping before testing a course.

See the deployment README for controls, logs and troubleshooting.

Figure 4. Microduck steers around cones using its 8×8 ToF sensor, with real footage on the left and a 3D rebuild from its logs on the right. Blue shows the policy steering, purple shows the operator intervention.

The Microduck task collection includes velocity tracking on flat and rough terrain; stand-up recovery, sit–stand transitions, and walking with fall recovery (VelStand); ball kicking, ground picking, and forward rolls (Roulade). Roller-skating tasks add velocity tracking and swizzle motion, crouch-gliding, slope descent, standing up on skates, and spins.

Figure 5. Fifteen Microduck task views: flat and rough-terrain walking, recovery, object interaction, and roller-skating motions.

Sources indicate that start with the first Microduck tutorial, then choose a task from the Microduck task collection to build your next policy in Isaac Lab with Newton. Explore fresh behaviors by changing commands, rewards, or environments—from rough-terrain walking to perception-driven obstacle avoidance. Evaluate your policy on scenes outside the training set before testing on the robot.

Recent findings suggest that view CSAF Summary Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. The EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody is used to enter or import the single line diagram, to get the extensive bill of material of your switchboard, including all devices, connection items, and mounting components. Failure to apply the remediations provided below may risk memory corruption, heap-based buffer overflow, and/or stack-based buffer overflow, which could result in local attackers being able to exploit these issues to potentially execute arbitrary code. The following versions of Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software are affected: EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software vers:generic/<=2.9.1.0_FR, 2.9.12.0101_FR, vers:generic/<=2.8.5.0301_ESP, 2.9.5.0000_ESP, vers:generic/<=2.8.7.0101_PT, 2.9.7.0000_PT, vers:generic/<=2.8.8.0201_BEL(FR), 2.9.8.0000_BELFR, vers:generic/<=2.8.3.0201_BEL(EN), 2.9.3.0000_BELEN, vers:generic/<=2.8.4.0401_INT(EN), 2.9.4.0000_INTEN, vers:generic/<=2.8.6.0000_INT(FR), 2.9.6.0000_INTFR, vers:generic/<=2.8.2.0000_NL, 2.9.6.0000_NL (CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055, CVE-2026-119055) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 5.3 Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software 1 Vulnerability Use After Free Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy, Critical Manufacturing, Commercial Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Tech giant Headquarters Location: France Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-119055 A CWE- 416: Use After Free vulnerability exists that could cause arbitrary code execution when a local attacker could trick the end user to open a specially crafted malicious SSD file. Schneider Electric CPCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. The EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody is used to enter or import the single line diagram, to get the extensive bill of material of your switchboard, including all devices, connection items, and mounting components. Failure to apply the remediations provided below may risk memory corruption, heap-based buffer overflow, and/or stack-based buffer overflow, which could result in local attackers being able to exploit these issues to potentially execute arbitrary code.

The following versions of Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software are affected:.
